title: Projected Cooling Degree Days (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Global Material Flows
description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Material Flows Database holds a variety of datasets on material extraction and consumption. The dataset displayed on Resource Watch shows global material consumption and extraction of nonmetallic minerals, biomass, fossil fuels, and metal ores at a national scale. This data is available at the source for every year between 1970 and 2017, but only the 2017 data is mapped on Resource Watch. The dataset also contains additional data on the overall consumption and extraction for each country at a per capita rate for the year 2015. Consumption and extraction are expressed in units of metric tons.  This dataset was created using national statistics from a combination of local government organizations and international organizations like the United Nations, Eurostat, and the United States Geological Survey.

  
  
This dataset was developed to assist governments in creating strategies to increase efficiency of material production and consumption activities. The dataset can help in better understanding how economic growth patterns influence resource use. It can also be used to evaluate the impacts of policies that have been adopted in the past. Additionally, the dataset can be used to develop effective strategies to minimize future resource use through targeted consumption and production policies. This database is used by academics around the world, integrated into several multi-regional input-output databases such as [EXIOBASE](https://www.exiobase.eu/) and featured in reports by international organisations, such as the United Nations Environmental Program and the European Economic Area.
  
  
This database was created by the United Nations Environment Programme International Resource Panel (UNEP IRP) and developed as part of a collaborative effort by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, the Sustainable Resource Use research group of the Vienna University of Economics and Business, the Institute of Social Ecology Vienna, the Nagoya University, and University of Sydney’s Integrated Sustainability Analysis.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was created by combining data from multiple sources. Data for all categories of extraction were taken from national production statistics. These datasets were collected from individual government ministries, industrial associations, and Eurostat's production statistics (PRODCOM) whenever available. Additional available data from international organizations, like the British Geological Survey and United States Geological Survey, were also used. Some categories, like metal ore extraction, were estimated using techniques in the [Eurostat: Economy-wide Material Flow Accounts Compilation Guide 2013](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/1798247/6191533/2013-EW-MFA-Guide-10Sep2013.pdf/). Data reported using different units was converted to a standard unit by using category-specific conversion factors.

  
  
Data on domestic material consumption was calculated by finding the sum of each country’s domestic extraction and import values and subtracting total exports. Data on imports and exports was taken from national offices when available and United Nations reports when not available. Both per capita datasets were created by dividing each country’s total extraction and consumption by its population. The final datasets were produced in tabular format at a national level.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for categories such as crops, natural gas and petroleum are available from the data provider. For each of these categories, data on trade, raw material consumption, raw material consumption per capita, raw material inputs, raw material equivalents of imports, raw material equivalents of exports is also provided. Lastly, data for each year from 1970 to 2017 is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

title: [Archived] Global Land Cover (IPCC Classification)
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](b2f00f99-46ed-43e6-a7a1-a5809d9369d4) as a replacement.**_
  
The Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Land Cover (LC) project of the European Space Agency (ESA) delivers consistent global LC maps at 300 m spatial resolution on an annual basis from 1992 to 2019. Each pixel value corresponds to the label of a land cover class defined based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) categories. This unique data set was produced thanks to the reprocessing and the interpretation of 5 different satellite missions.   
  
Baseline LC maps are generated thanks to the entire MERIS FR and RR archive from 2003 through 2012. Independently from this baseline, LC changes are detected at 1 km based on the AVHRR time series between 1992 to 1999, SPOT-VGT time series between 1999 and 2013, and PROBA-V data from 2013. When MERIS FR or PROBA-V time series are available, changes detected at 1 km are remapped at 300 m. The last step consists in back- and updating the 10-year baseline LC map to produce the 28 annual LC maps from 1992 to 2019. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: [Archived] Vulnerability to Climate Change Index
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](4d2d47c1-fed1-4484-83e3-c91c3f6f7315) as a replacement.**_
  
The University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) produces an annual index of climate change adaptation potential annually from 1995 to 2015. A country's ND-GAIN score is composed of a vulnerability score and a readiness score. Vulnerability and readiness are based on compiled indicators. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. ND-GAIN measures overall vulnerability by considering 6 life-supporting sectors—food, water, health, ecosystem service, human habitat, and infrastructure—and 36 indicators. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. ND-GAIN measures overall readiness by considering 3 components—economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness—and 9 indicators. Each indicator comes from a public data source. Infrastructure Investment Outlook
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from the Global Infrastructure Hub (GI Hub) shows national infrastructure investment gaps in 2015 U.S. dollars for the following sectors: energy, telecommunications, airports, ports, rail, road, and water. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total sectors.  
  
An investment gap represents the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued.The investment gap of a country where the investment trends meet their future investment needs is zero.  
  
This dataset was developed by the Global Infrastructure Hub. The data covers a total of 56 countries for the years 2016 to 2040.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Global Infrastructure Outlook was calculated using a “top-down” approach, beginning with existing cross-country datasets on infrastructure spending and filling in data gaps, where necessary. Sources for the initial cross-country datasets include the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Infrastructure in Latin America (INFRALATAM), and Eurostat.  
  
The infrastructure investment gap for each year was calculated as the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued for that year.  
  
Gaps in national data were filled using data from national statistics agencies and major infrastructure companies. In areas where no data sources could be identified, econometric estimation was used to compute values. In countries where a time series existed but was incomplete, further manipulation was often required to fill in the gaps in that series. For data gaps in the middle of a time series, interpolation was used to fill the gaps. When data was missing from the beginning or the end of the time series, forecasting and/or backcasting were used to develop a longer time series.  
  
In the case where data was attributed to a broader sector, secondary data sources were used to align the data with the preferred sector definition. In some countries, data related to investment in utilities was used to attribute the investment into more detailed sectors like water and energy. For example, if energy accounts for 60% of the country's utilities investment, then 60% of the utilities investment would be allocated to the energy sector.  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://cdn.gihub.org/outlook/live/methodology/Global+Infrastructure+Outlook+-+July+2017.pdf).

title: Wetlands
description:
This data set estimates large-scale wetland distributions and important wetland complexes, including areas of marsh, fen, peatland, and water (Lehner and Döll 2004). Large rivers are also included as wetlands (lotic wetlands); it is assumed that only a river with adjacent wetlands (floodplain) is wide enough to appear as a polygon on the coarse-scale source maps. Wetlands are a crucial part of natural infrastructure as they help protect water quality, hold excess flood water, stabilize shoreline, and help recharge groundwater (Beeson and Doyle 1995, Stuart and Edwards 2006). Limited by sources, the data set refers to lakes as permanent still-water bodies (lentic water bodies) without direct connection to the sea, including saline lakes and lagoons as lakes, while excluding intermittent or ephemeral water bodies. Lakes that are manmade are explicitly classified as reservoirs. The Global Lakes and Wetlands Database combines best available sources for lakes and wetlands on a global scale. This data set includes information on large lakes (area ≥ 50 km2) and reservoirs (storage capacity ≥ 0.5 km3), permanent open water bodies (surface area ≥ 0.1 km2), and maximum extent and types of wetlands. title: Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels
description:
### Overview  
  
The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset shows the species richness and number of threatened species for amphibians and mammals. Species richness is defined by the number of mammal or amphibian species present in a given area. The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) [Red List](https://www.iucnredlist.org/about/background-history) defines a [threatened species](https://www.iucn.org/resources/conservation-tools/iucn-red-list-threatened-species) as one that is threatened with global extinction (critically endangered, endangered, or vulnerable). The Red List is the world’s most comprehensive list of species status and extinction risk, with assessments for over 120,000 species. The data shown here evaluated 5,198 amphibian species and 5,488 mammalian species in 2013. Gridded data is available at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds, which is approximately 1 kilometer (km) x 1 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.

  
  
Biodiversity – the variety of life on earth – is essential to a healthy and stable environment. Biodiversity conservation is critical for food supply, fighting climate change, and providing natural resources for humans. However, human activities such as pollution, farming and deforestation have negatively impacted biodiversity, causing the loss of species and their habitats. Amphibians are facing the highest rates of decline: almost 50% of amphibian species are threatened, primarily in South America and Southeast Asia. Similarly, almost 50% of mammal species are in decline and 20% are threatened. Marine mammals are among the most threatened species. The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset is an important tool for wildlife conservation efforts. Understanding the magnitude and geographic focus of threatened species is important for making policy decisions and allocating conservation resources. Additionally, this dataset can be used for biodiversity modeling studies and understanding human interactions with the environment. 

  
  
Founded in 1948, the [International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN)](https://www.iucn.org/about) comprises more than 1,400 governmental and civil member organizations. Its mission is to influence, encourage and assist conservation of natural diversity, and ensure that the use of any natural resources is equitable and sustainable. The IUCN provides the Red List as a tool to inform conservation decisions and protect the natural resources necessary for human life. The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Level dataset was aggregated by [Columbia University’s Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN)](http://www.ciesin.columbia.edu/) using data from the IUCN Red List. CIESIN specializes in online data management and spatial data integration for interdisciplinary research related to human interactions with the environment.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Amphibian and Mammalian Richness and Threat Levels dataset was created from species distribution shapefiles from the IUCN Red List. The shapefile data is from 2013 and has a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds (approximately 1 km at the equator). The number in each grid cell represents the number of species present or the number of species threatened within that cell. 

  
  
CIESIN created the richness and threat level rasters by converting the shapefiles to GeoTIFF rasters based on attributes from the IUCN data. Amphibian and mammalian richness maps were created by aggregating individual species maps with the **Extant** class attribute. This attribute refers to species that are currently surviving in the wild. Threat level maps were created in the same way using the **All Threats** IUCN threat category. The All Threats category includes species classified as Critically Endangered (extremely high risk of extinction in the wild), Endangered (very high risk of extinction in the wild ) or Vulnerable (high risk of extinction in the wild). Species within these categories are undergoing reversible declines in population, geographic extent, habitat, and mature individuals. Red List species assessments follow a specific set of guidelines and undergo review before publication. More information about the Red List assessment process can be found [here](https://www.iucnredlist.org/assessment/process).

Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22).   
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Heating Degree Days
description:
A heating degree day (HDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is below 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined HDD for those two days would be 30. HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. 

This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from heating in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts.

This data set shows HDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Environmental Democracy Index
description:
The Environmental Democracy Index (EDI) was developed by The Access Initiative (TAI) and World Resources Institute (WRI) in collaboration with partners around the world. The index evaluates 70 countries, across 75 legal indicators, based on objective and internationally recognized standards established by the Bali Guidelines of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP). Legal indicators test both the extent of provisions that promote environmental democracy and the strength of a given provision in providing an enforceable legal right for the public. Each of these indicators is scored on a range from 0 (lowest) to 3 (highest). A score of 3 means that the respective provision exemplifies accepted good practice. A score of 2 indicates that a majority—but not all—of environmental decision-making includes a certain provision, or indicates moderately strong provision. A score of 1 translates to a weaker provision that grants significant discretion to government agencies to fulfil these rights, or that a right only applies to a minority of environmental decision-making processes. A score of 0 indicates that the law is either silent or prohibits some aspect of procedural rights, depending on the indicator. The overall EDI score is the average of the scores of the 75 legal indicators. The EDI also includes a supplemental set of 24 limited practice indicators that provide insight on a country’s performance in implementation. The national laws and practices were assessed and scored by more than 140 lawyers around the world. Country assessments were conducted in 2014 and will be updated every 2 years. title: Gender Gap Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The Gender Gap Index quantifies the gaps between women and men in four key areas: health, education, economy, and politics. Data is available from 149 countries for select years between 2010-2021. Scores are based on the level of access women have to resources and opportunities relative to men. Countries are given a score from 0-1. A score of 1 indicates full equality between women and men and a score of 0 indicates full inequality. The Gender Gap Index is published annually by the World Economic Forum (WEF) and is designed to capture the magnitude of gender-based disparities and track progress over time.

Gender equality is a necessity for a peaceful, prosperous and sustainable world. Women represent half of the world’s population but continue to be underrepresented in leadership and in the workplace. According to the 2021 Gender Gap Index, only 27% of global managerial positions were held by women in 2021. The largest gap between women and men was in political empowerment, where only 26.1% of about 35,500 parliament seats and 22.6% of over 3,400 ministers globally are held by women. The Gender Gap Index serves as a benchmark for comparing countries and their progress to gender equality over time. Based on current trends, the WEF estimates that it will take 135.6 years to close the global gender gap. However, the 2021 Gender Gap Index shows that many countries have made significant progress towards closing the gender gap. These countries include Iceland, Finland, Norway, New Zealand, Sweden, Namibia, Rwanda, and Lithuania.

The WEF Centre for the New Economy and Society published the Gender Gap Index. The WEF is an international NGO founded in 1971. Focused on public-private cooperation, the WEF brings together political, business and cultural leaders at their annual meetings, workshops and seminars. The WEF’s primary aim is to drive positive change for the world by conducting research, producing data and leading collaborative projects and initiatives. The Centre for the New Economy and Society is focused on closing economic gender gaps, fostering diversity and promoting inclusive growth.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Gender Gap Index quantified the gaps between men and women across four subindexes: economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment. Indicators were scored within each subindex. The Gender Gap Index was based on three underlying concepts that determined how indicators were chosen, how the data was treated and how the index can be used. These concepts can be thought of as the “rules” for how the subindexes were scored.
  
  
First, the index measured gender-based gaps in access to resources and opportunities in countries, rather than the actual levels of the available resources and opportunities. This rewarded countries with smaller gaps in access to these resources, regardless of the overall level of resources. Second, the index evaluated countries based on outcomes rather than inputs. Inputs – indicators related to country-specific policies, rights or customs – were not included in the index. For example, the gap between women and men in high-skilled jobs (an outcome indicator) was measured, but the length of maternity leave (a country-specific policy) was not. Third, the index evaluated countries based on their proximity to gender equality, rather than their level of women’s empowerment. The index rewarded countries in which outcomes for women equaled those for men, but it neither rewarded nor penalized countries in which women outperformed men. 

  
  
The four subindexes were scored based on the following indicators: 
- Economic participation and opportunity: This subindex measured gender-based gaps in workforce participation, remuneration and advancement. The remuneration gap was measured by the ratio of estimated female-to-male earned income and a qualitative assessment of wage equality for similar work. The advancement gap was captured through two hard data statistics: the ratio of women to men among legislators, senior officials and managers, and the ratio of women to men among technical and professional workers. Data was provided by the [International Labour Organization ILOSTAT database](https://ilostat.ilo.org/) and the WEF. 
- Educational attainment: Gender-based gaps in educational attainment were measured with the ratio of women to men enrolled in primary, secondary and tertiary education. The ratio of female to male literacy was also used as an indicator of a country’s long-term ability to educate women and men. Data was provided by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Institute for Statistics Education Indicators database](http://uis.unesco.org/).
- Health and survival: The differences between women’s and men’s health were measured using the sex ratio at birth and the gap between women’s and men’s healthy life expectancy. Sex ratio at birth is the measure of male births for every female birth and was included to capture the phenomenon of [“missing women.”](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/10/where-are-all-the-women/) This refers to the observation of a low ratio of women to men, particularly in countries with a strong son preference. Data for this subindex was provided by the [United Nations (UN) World Population Prospects dataset](https://population.un.org/wpp/) and the [World Health Organization (WHO) Global Health Observatory database](https://www.who.int/data/gho).
- Political empowerment: The gap between women and men at the highest level of political decision-making was measured by the ratio of women to men in ministerial positions and the ratio of women to men in parliamentary positions. The ratio of women to men in terms of years in executive office (prime minister or president) for the last 50 years was also included. Data was provided by the Inter-Parliamentary Union [Women in National Parliaments](http://archive.ipu.org/wmn-e/classif.htm).  [Women in Politics](https://www.ipu.org/resources/publications/infographics/2020-03/women-in-politics-2020) datasets and the WEF. 

  
  
All data was converted to female-to-male ratios. Ratios were then truncated at the “equality benchmark”. The equality benchmark was 1 for all indicators except the two in the health subindex. The sex ratio at birth equality benchmark was 0.9445 and the healthy life expectancy benchmark was 1.06. Truncating ratios at 1 assigns the same score to a country that has reached equality between women and men (a ratio of 1) and one in which women have surpassed men (a ratio greater than 1). This method measured how close women were to achieving equality with men in a country, but did not reward or penalize countries with a gender gap in the opposite direction. The total score for each subindex was a weighted average of the scores for each indicator. A weighted average was used to make sure each indicator had the same relative impact on the total score.The overall score for each country was a simple average of the subindex scores. A score of 0 indicated complete inequality between women and men and a score of 1 indicated complete equality.  

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://reports.weforum.org/global-gender-gap-report-2018/measuring-the-global-gender-gap/).

description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2019, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality. 

  
  
The 2019 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. The GHI classifies countries by the following severity layers: low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger.   
  
### Methodology  
  
GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger.
  
  

First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators:
  
  
1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient);
  
  
2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition);
  
  
3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and
  
  
4. Child mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments).
  
  

Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades.
  
  

Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight.
  
  

This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores.

title: Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for black carbon (BC). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources.

  
  
Black carbon is the sooty black material emitted from gas and diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, and other sources that burn fossil fuel. It is made up of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) that is 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter. PM2.5 can have significant health risks for people with compromised respiratory systems, the young, and the old. Black carbon is a global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate. Inhalation of black carbon is associated with health problems including respiratory and cardiovascular disease, cancer, and even birth defects. Black carbon also contributes to climate change causing changes in patterns of rain and clouds.

  
  
OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The black carbon station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria:

  
  
1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site.
  
  
2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region.
  
  
3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours.

  
  
After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25).

Cropland and Pasture Area
description:
### Overview  
  
The Cropland and Pasture Area dataset shows the global distribution of agricultural activities for the year 2000. It is a combination of both satellite based datasets and agricultural inventory data from censuses. The dataset displays the percentage of land used for farming (cropland) and livestock (pasture area) for each grid cell. Each grid cell has a value of 0% to 100% coverage. A value of 0% means there are no agricultural activities present and 100% means the gridcell is completely used for cropland or pasture area. The dataset is displayed at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (around 10 kilometers).
  
  

The Cropland and Pasture Area dataset was created by EarthStat with assistance from the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE), and the Land Use and Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC). It was created to help understand the positive social and economic benefits, as well as the negative environmental consequences, of agricultural land use. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Cropland and Pasture Area in 2000 dataset was created by combining two different high-resolution satellite based land cover datasets and agricultural inventory data. The agricultural inventory data is allocated to the 10 kilometer resolution using the higher resolution land cover datasets and statistical modeling. 
  
  

The two satellite based land cover datasets used were the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Land Cover Type Product and the Satellite Pour l’Observation de la Terre (SPOT) VEGETATION based Global Land Cover 2000 (GLC2000) dataset. The MODIS dataset was created with data collected from October 2000 to October 2001 and was analyzed using remote imaging with a globally consistent classification scheme. The SPOT dataset was created with data from November 1999 to December 2000 and used a variable land use classification scheme that included information from regional institutions. Both datasets have a spatial resolution of about 1 kilometer. A single land cover dataset was created by overlaying the MODIS and GLC2000 datasets, where each classification was the combination of the MODIS and GLC2000 classifications. This combination land cover product was found to provide more accurate results when calibrated against the inventory data, as opposed to using either data set individually.
  
  

Cropland and pasture inventory data was compiled for the globe at the national and subnational level for circa year 2000. This resulted in compiled data for 15,990 different administrative units of the world, ranging from political units like countries, states and counties. Inventory data was found from either census data or the Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) [FAOSTAT database](http://faostat.fao.org). The cropland and pasture data was compiled to be consistent with the FAO definition of “Arable lands and permanent crops” and “Permanent pastures” respectively. The agricultural inventory data were seldom available exactly for the year 2000, therefore the authors collected inventory data between the years 1998 to 2002 where possible, but in several instances relied on older data.
  
  
 
Information within the final Cropland and Pasture Area dataset for areas that were clearly non-agricultural (tundra, boreal forest, and protected land) were masked to reduce the possibility of misclassification. For full information, please see the source [methodology](http://www.earthstat.org/cropland-pasture-area-2000/).

In addition, a set of historical data based on HYDE, and multiple alternative scenarios of the future (2015-2100) developed by Integrated Assessment Model (IAM) teams, are being developed as input for these models. The goal of the Land-Use Harmonization (LUH2) project is to prepare a harmonized set of land-use scenarios that smoothly connects the historical reconstructions of land-use with the future projections in the format required for ESMs. The land-use harmonization strategy estimates the global fractional land-use patterns, underlying land-use transitions, and key agricultural management information, annually for the time period 850-2100 at 0.25° x 0.25° resolution, while minimizing the differences at the transition between the historical reconstruction ending conditions and IAM initial conditions, and working to preserve changes depicted by the IAMs in the future. description:
The GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP) was created by NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) and is now run by NOAA's Earth System Research Laboratory Physical Sciences Division (ESRL-PSD). GISTEMP provides an estimate of global surface and air temperature changes. The basic GISS temperature analysis scheme was defined by James Hansen in the late 1970s, when a method of estimating global temperature change was needed for comparison with 1-dimensional global climate models. The scheme was based on the finding that the correlation of temperature change was reasonably strong for stations separated by up to 1,200 km, especially at middle and high latitudes. This fact proved sufficient to obtain useful estimates for global mean temperature changes. The analysis method was fully documented in Hansen and Lebedeff (1987), including quantitative estimates of the error in annual and 5-year mean temperature change. This was done by sampling at station locations a spatially complete data set of a long run of a global climate model, which was shown to have realistic spatial and temporal variability. This however only addresses the error due to incomplete spatial coverage of measurements. As there are other potential sources of error, such as urban warming near meteorological stations, many other methods have been used to verify the approximate magnitude of inferred global warming. These methods include inference of surface temperature change from vertical temperature profiles in the ground (bore holes) at many sites around the world, rate of glacier retreat at many locations, and studies by several groups of the effect of urban and other local human influences on the global temperature record. All of these yield consistent estimates of the approximate magnitude of global warming, which reached about 0.8°C in 2010, twice the magnitude reported in 1981. Further affirmation of the reality of the warming is its spatial distribution, which has largest values at locations remote from any local human influence, with a global pattern consistent with that expected for response to global climate forcings (larger in the Northern Hemisphere than the Southern Hemisphere, larger at high latitudes than low latitudes, larger over land than over ocean). More recent documentation compares alternative analyses and addresses questions about perception and reality of global warming; various choices for the ocean data are tested; it is also shown that global temperature change is sensitive to estimated temperature change in polar regions, where observations are limited. A multiyear smoothing is applied to fully remove the annual cycle and improve information content in temperature graphs. Despite large year-to-year fluctuations associated with the El Niño-La Niña cycle of tropical ocean temperature, the conclusion could be drawn that global temperature continued to rise rapidly in the 21st century, new record heights being reached in every decade. One of the improvements—introduced in 1998—was the implementation of a method to address the problem of urban warming: The urban and periurban (i.e., other than rural) stations are adjusted so that their long-term trend matches that of the mean of neighboring rural stations. Urban stations without nearby rural stations are dropped. This preserves local short-term variability without affecting long-term trends. Originally, the classification of stations was based on population size near that station; the current analysis uses satellite-observed night-lights to determine which stations are located in urban and periurban areas. description:
### Overview  
  
The biodiversity intactness map shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in an area. This data is important because if biodiversity loss goes unchecked, it will undermine efforts toward long-term sustainable development. The data, created by [Newbold et al. (2016)](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288), represents intactness in 2005 at a 1 kilometer resolution.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The Biodiversity Intactness dataset shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in samples from local terrestrial ecological assemblages. The map represents the average losses of originally present species. The datasets used 2,382,624 data points from the Projecting Responses of Ecological Diversity in Changing Terrestrial Systems (PREDICTS) database, a global database of how local terrestrial biodiversity responds to human impacts. The map modeled how richness and abundance respond to land use pressures. The models included 4 pressure variables—land use, land use intensity, human population density, and proximity to the nearest road. The values of the response variables were expressed relative to an intact assemblage undisturbed by humans. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288).

FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index measures how restrictive foreign direct investment (FDI) is in a country. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is an investment made by an entity in one country into another country’s business interests. FDI is particularly important in developing countries and emerging markets as it can provide capital for technology and infrastructure and create jobs for local workers. However, some countries that receive foreign investment impose restrictions on FDI. For a given country, the four main FDI restrictions in each economic sector were evaluated and scored based on how discriminatory they are to foreign investors. These restrictions are foreign equity limitations; screening and approval requirements; restrictions on foreign key personnel; and other operational restrictions. Scores range from 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions). The scores of each sector were averaged to calculate the country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. This dataset includes FDI data from 22 economic sectors for OECD and G20 countries and is updated annually.
  
  
The index captures a country’s ability to attract FDI. It can also be used to measure changes in regulatory restrictions over time and how these changes affect FDI inflow. Highly restrictive countries receive less FDI compared to less restrictive countries with similarly sized economies. FDI restrictions can be costly to governments in terms of loss of potential investments. They also increase costs in service sectors and negatively impact stocks. Studies of this dataset have shown that countries that reform FDI restrictions attract more foreign investors. FDI restrictions reform can positively impact developing countries by promoting economic growth and investment in human capital. 
  
  
The OECD created the FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. The OECD is an international organization founded in 1961. The 36 member states work to shape policies that foster prosperity, equality, opportunity and well-being.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The FDI Regulatory Restrictions Index uses data from 22 economic sectors. Economic sectors include industries like agriculture, media, electricity, transportation and financial services. 
  
  
Scoring for each sector was based on the following restriction types:
Limits on the amount of foreign equity ownership permitted
Screening and approval procedures applied to inward foreign direct investment
Restrictions on the employment of foreigners as key personnel
Other restrictions (e.g., land ownership, reciprocity requirements, access to local finance)
  
  
Scoring was based on the discriminatory nature of a country’s measures, i.e. whether the measures applied to only foreign investors. Restrictions were evaluated on a 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions) scale. The restrictiveness of each sector was calculated by adding the scores for each of the four types of FDI restrictions (with a maximum score of 1). A country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index is the average of the scores from all 22 economic sectors. 

  
  
The score for **foreign equity limits** differentiated between three key thresholds: full exclusion of foreign participation, restrictions on foreign majority control and limits on full foreign ownership. The score further distinguished between start-up businesses and takeovers. If the measure only applied to takeovers, the score was reduced by half. **Screening and approval mechanisms** that applied only to foreign investors were scored based on a monetary threshold. Restrictive countries required approval of new FDI/acquisitions worth less than $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Less restrictive countries did not require approval of new FDI/acquisitions until they exceeded $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Open countries required no screening, only pre-notification from foreign investors. Restrictions on **foreign key personnel** were scored on two criteria: limitations on foreign employment and board of directors members. The OECD defines key personnel as employees in a managerial role or employees with essential technical skills. Restrictive countries did not allow employment of foreign key personnel. Less restrictive countries imposed time limits or required economic justification of foreign key personnel employment. Nationality/residence requirements for board of directors members are common. Restrictive countries required the majority of board members to be citizens. In contrast, less restrictive countries required only one board member to be a citizen. **Other restrictions** are measures that could affect the potential operations of foreign investors. These include restrictions on the following: land ownership, access to local finance, capital/profit repatriation, and establishment of local branches. title: Gender Inequality Index
description:
The Gender Inequality Index (GII), released by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), is an inequality index for 159 countries from 1995 to 2015. It measures gender inequalities and is calculated using 3 important aspects of human development: (1) reproductive health, measured by maternal mortality ratio and adolescent birth rates; (2) empowerment, measured by proportion of parliamentary seats occupied by females and proportion of adult females and males aged 25 years and older with at least some secondary education; and (3) economic status, expressed as labor market participation and measured by labor force participation rate of female and male populations aged 15 and older. The index ranges from 0, where women and men fare equally, to 1, where one gender fares as poorly as possible in all measured dimensions. The higher the GII value, the more disparities between females and males and the more loss to human development. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas
description:
### Overview  
  
The Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas dataset, produced by National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, models human sewage inputs into coastal waters for the year 2015. When human sewage flows into coastal waters it contributes to increased nitrogen levels and pathogens in coastal systems. This dataset quantifies and maps the flow of nitrogen and pathogen input to the ocean from nearly 135,000 watersheds using a high-resolution geospatial model. The sources of nitrogen inputs are separated by source into treated (sewered systems), septic, and untreated (open defecation) inputs. The dataset provides global rasters of the modeled plume, or extent, of the nitrogen in coastal waters. Nitrogen plume data is shown at ~1 km resolution. 

  
  
Human sewage is considered both an ecological and a human health issue because it contributes both increased levels of nitrogen and pathogens to coastal waters. Excess nitrogen plays a key role in the ecological degradation of coastal ecosystems through a process called [eutrophication](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/eutrophication.html). Eutrophication leads to harmful algal blooms and low-oxygen waters, which can kill fish, and degrade essential fish habitats. Pathogens in coastal waters can promote disease in marine organisms, such as coral reefs, and can cause human health impacts. It is important to monitor both nitrogen and pathogen concentrations, to understand trends and inform management.  

  
  
The National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis created this dataset to inform marine conservation and public health work. The model allows for the comparison of global models of nitrogen sources with traditional water quality monitoring to identify priority hotspots. In-depth local monitoring can then pinpoint the true sources of and quantities of pollutants like nitrogen to benefit conservation and management. The model also links nitrogen inputs with data on pathogens in coastal waters to inform policy decisions around wastewater treatment options. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Nitrogen concentration (grams/yr) was modeled using a high-resolution geospatial model. Population and settlement data were grouped into rural and urban classes. These data were then combined with national-level statistics on protein consumption and the proportion of the population’s access to various types of wastewater treatment facilities. Wastewater treatment types were grouped into three categories - open defecation (untreated), septic tanks (septic), or some level of sewered treatment. The three sewage treatment categories of nitrogen were assigned a nitrogen removal efficiency based on literature. The model assumed that populations with inputs from septic tanks or open defecation that are more than 1km away from surface waters and coastlines do not contribute to effluent totals. 

  
  
The dispersion of the wastewater pollution into the ocean was then modeled from each basin’s pourpoint, which describes the location where freshwater enters the ocean. For each watershed with a pourpoint draining into the ocean, nitrogen inputs were calculated by summing the values for all grid cells falling within the watershed boundary and this value was assigned to the corresponding coastal pourpoint. At each pourpoint, the level of nitrogen was spread into the coastal waters using a plume model based on a logarithmic decay function. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0258898#sec002).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also provides data on nitrogen inputs at the watershed level in [Watersheds Transporting Wastewater to Coastal Ocean](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/784732cc-8e7e-4dac-be51-d4506ff2ee04) and for the associated coastal “pourpoint” or the location where the watershed empties into the ocean in  [Wastewater Inputs to Coastal Areas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5bf349ec-3b14-4021-a7d4-fc4b8104bd74).

Fishing Activity
description:
### Overview  
  
The Apparent Fishing Effort dataset, produced by Global Fishing Watch (GFW), shows the distribution of time spent fishing in different locations throughout the ocean at a 0.01 degree resolution between 2012 and 2021. The time spent fishing in each pixel is tracked using a maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS).

  
  
Commercial fishing is a vital part of the global economy and is crucial to the food security and cultural identity of millions of people. However some practices, like trawling and dredging, destroy far more ocean habitat than any other fishing practice. When dredging or trawling, commercial vessels drag a dredge or heavy net, respectively, along the seafloor to scrape up species like oysters or shrimp. The process of scraping the seafloor is extremely destructive to deep-sea marine ecosystems, productivity, biodiversity, and carbon storage. Historically, practices like trawling and dredging have been difficult and costly to monitor, but technology and transparency are driving tangible change in how the sector is managed. 

  
  
Global Fishing Watch is advancing ocean governance through increased transparency of human activity at sea. By creating and publicly sharing map visualizations, data and analysis tools, they enable scientific research and drive a transformation in how we manage our ocean. By 2030, they aim to monitor and visualize the impact of ocean-going vessels, both industrial and small-scale, that are responsible for the vast majority of the global seafood catch.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Global Fishing Watch’s apparent fishing effort dataset is based on transmissions broadcast using publicly available automatic identification system (AIS) information. AIS is a GPS-like device that large ships use to broadcast their position in order to avoid collisions. Each year, more than 400,000 AIS devices broadcast vessel location along with other information on vessel identity, course and speed. Ground stations and satellites pick up this information, meaning a ship’s movements can be followed even in the most remote parts of the ocean. 

  
  
GFW uses two convolutional neural networks (CNN)—a cutting edge form of machine learning model—to help classify fishing vessels (vessel characterization model) and predict when they are fishing (fishing detection model). They first [identify fishing vessels](https://globalfishingwatch.org/datasets-and-code-vessel-identity/) by combining a comprehensive database of vessel registry information with the output of the vessel characterization model to predict features like geartype and size. Next, GFW estimates where and when each vessel is fishing based on its movement patterns. The fishing detection model was trained using over a thousand manually labeled vessel tracks to learn what fishing movements look like. This model predicts a score for every AIS position in the database to distinguish fishing positions from non-fishing positions, such as during vessel transits. When the fishing detection model scores an AIS position as a fishing position, the time associated with that AIS position is considered apparent fishing activity. For more information about the two models, please see the supplementary materials of the [associated paper](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646).

  
  
After identifying fishing vessels and detecting fishing positions in the AIS data, apparent fishing effort can be calculated for any area by summarizing the fishing hours for all fishing vessels in that area. Global Fishing Watch’s fishing detection algorithm is a best effort mathematically to identify “apparent fishing activity.” As a result, it is possible that some fishing activity is not identified as such by Global Fishing Watch; conversely, Global Fishing Watch may show apparent fishing activity where fishing is not actually taking place. 

  
  
 To generate maps of apparent fishing effort GFW “rasterizes” the AIS positions by placing them into a grid and calculating the total fishing activity in each grid cell. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646)
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. This map displays effort by all vessels other than trawlers or dredgers. Resource Watch shows separate GFW data for [Trawling Activity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6ccfb266-20cd-4838-82b0-5309987a62f0). [Data disaggregated by flag state, vessel, and gear type](https://globalfishingwatch.org/data-download/datasets/public-fishing-effort) is also available through Global Fishing Watch. 

  
  
For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team requested a visualization of the data through the Global Fishing Watch API. This visualization powered by 4-Wings, Global Fishing Watch experimental technology for rapid access to global
scale temporal data sets. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github.](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_030a_rw1_fishing_activity)

description:
The Annual Precipitation data set was adapted from the University of California, Berkeley's WorldClim V1 Bioclim, which produces bioclimatic variables derived from the monthly temperature and rainfall in order to generate more biologically meaningful values. The data product covers the period January 1, 1960, to December 31, 1990, and has global coverage at 1 km resolution. The bioclimatic variables represent annual trends (e.g., mean annual temperature, annual precipitation), seasonality (e.g., annual range in temperature and precipitation), and extreme or limiting environmental factors (e.g., temperature of the coldest and warmest month, and precipitation of the wettest and driest quarters). Climate data sets were created based on data from various sources, including the Global Historical Climate Network data set, the World Meteorological Organization's Climatological Normals (CLINO), the FAOCLIM 2.0 global climate database, the International Center for Tropical Agriculture, and various regional climate databases. The data set contains the following bands: Annual Mean Temperature; Mean Diurnal Range; Isothermality; Temperature Seasonality; Max Temperature of Warmest Month; Min Temperature of Coldest Month; Temperature Annual Range; Mean Temperature of Wettest Quarter; Mean Temperature of Driest Quarter; Mean Temperature of Warmest Quarter; Mean Temperature of Coldest Quarter; Annual Precipitation; Precipitation of Wettest Month (mm); Precipitation of Driest Month (mm); Precipitation Seasonality; Precipitation of Wettest Quarter (mm); Precipitation of Driest Quarter (mm); Precipitation of Warmest Quarter (mm); and Precipitation of Coldest Quarter (mm). This scheme follows that of ANUCLIM, except that for temperature seasonality the standard deviation was used because a coefficient of variation does not make sense with temperatures between -1 and 1. title: Positive Peace Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The Positive Peace Index (PPI) is a quantitative approach to measure Positive Peace. Positive Peace is defined as the attitudes, institutions, and structures that lead to a more peaceful society. A country with a higher PPI is more capable of building and maintaining peace. 

  
  
The Positive Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure a country’s success in building and maintaining peace.  Positive peace is used to create resilient and adaptive communities that prevent conflict and help societies channel disagreements productively. The framework for PPI is based on eight domains:

  
  
1. *Acceptance of the Rights of Others:* This requires countries to have formal laws that can guarantee basic human rights and freedoms, ensure gender equality, and worker’s rights.
  
  
2. *Equitable Distribution of Resources:* This ensures everyone has equal access to resources, such as education and health.
  
  
3. *Free Flow of Information:* This is measured by the extent to which citizens can gain access to information, whether the media is free and independent, and how well-informed citizens are.
  
  
4. *Good Relations with Neighbours:* A country’s relationship with other countries is an important indicator of how peaceful and politically stable the country is.
  
  
5. *High Levels of Human Capital:*  The employment rate among young citizens and the number of people engaged in research activities shows the level of social capital in a country.
  
  
6. *Low Levels of Corruption:*  High levels of corruption leads to a shortage of funding for essential services, which creates unrest in a society.
  
  
7. *Sound Business Environment:*  This is measured by the presence of regulatory systems and formal institutions in a country to support a good business environment.
  
  
8. *Well-Functioning Government:*  A government that delivers high-quality public and civil services, creates trust and participation, maintains political stability, and promotes the rule of law is necessary for a peaceful country.

  
  
The PPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2009 to 2018 for 163 countries covering 99.6% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand and make progress towards global peacefulness along with other interrelated areas such as:  improved economic productivity and social advancement.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Positive Peace Index (PPI) uses 24 indicators in eight domains to measure Positive Peace. The eight domains range from the flow of information within a country to levels of corruption. PPI is interconnected to the Global Peace Index (GPI) which is another measurement for global peacefulness. GPI is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence in a country. The internal measures of the Global Peace Index were statistically compared to approximately 25,000 national data series, indices, and attitudinal surveys to determine the initial set of indicators for Positive Peace Index. These indicators were then qualitatively assessed. If there were multiple indicators for similar cases, the least important ones were discarded. 

  
  
Finally, the remaining indicators were aggregated into the eight domains of Positive Peace and given a correlation coefficient to their value in GPI using statistical approaches. The correlation coefficient represented how important the indicators were in the PPI measurement compared to GPI. The correlation coefficient was used to weight GPI Internal Peace scores for each indicator and create a final score out of 5.  For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/10/PPR-2019-web.pdf).

title: India Projected Change in Average Temperature
description:
This dataset, available from the Centre for Climate Change Research (CCCR) at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), shows projected change in average temperature over the Indian subcontinent. 

These downscaled climate scenarios contain high resolution downscaled projections of regional climate and monsoon over South Asia until 2100 for the IPCC using the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) at 50 km horizontal resolution. The projections are an ensemble of six member global climate models from the CMIP5, which help drive the regional model with lateral and lower boundary conditions. The IITM-RegCM4 regional climate model outputs are archived by CCCR-IITM in the framework of the WCRP regional activity Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX; http://www.cordex.org), and are disseminated to users and stakeholders for application studies and impact assessments by publishing on the CCCR-IITM Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) data node (see more details at http://cccr.tropmet.res.in/home/cordexsa_datasets.jsp).

Projected change in average temperature is computed using daily mean near-surface air temperature in degrees Celsius for the historical period (1951-2005) and for future projections (2006-2099) based on two Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) scenarios (RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) of the IPCC. These indicators are then used to derive an ensemble mean (average of the 6 IITM-RegCM4 model members). These are presented as the future changes in three 30-year period: short-term (2016-2045), mid-term (2036-2065), and long-term (2066-2095) averages relative to the baseline 30-year period (1976-2005) average.

The daily fields from 1951 to 2099 for each member model available in netCDF4 file format are processed to compute the climate indicators (30-year averages) using the Climate Data Operators (CDO; https://code.mpimet.mpg.de/projects/cdo), which is a collection of command line operators to manipulate and analyze climate model data. The processed climate indicators available in netCDF4 file format can be visualized using the Grid Analysis and Display System (GrADS; http://cola.gmu.edu/grads), an interactive desktop tool that is used for easy access, manipulation, and visualization of earth science data.
