title: Extreme Heat Days
description:
Extreme heat days represent the annual average count of days with heat greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP).

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Satellite Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: NO₂ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) density in the troposphere. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of NO₂ between Earth’s surface and the top of the troposphere. The NO₂ density is reported with units of moles of NO₂ per square meter of air (mol/m²).

  
  
Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is one of the most common compounds in the nitrogen oxides (NOx) group. Other nitrogen oxides include nitric acid (HNO₃) and nitric oxide (NO). NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides, meaning if NO₂ is present it is likely other nitrogen oxides are as well. NO₂ is primarily created by the burning of fuel, which can be from cars, trucks and buses, power plants, and off-road equipment. Breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the human respiratory system. Acute exposures can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms, like coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing. Longer chronic exposures to elevated concentrations of NO₂ may contribute to the development of asthma and potentially increase susceptibility to respiratory infections. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂.

  
  
The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system. The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to  provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as NO₂, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The TROPOMI NO₂ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. The data was retrieved and analyzed using a 3 step process. 

  
  
1. Total NO₂ slant column density was determined from radiance and irradiance spectra measured by TROPOMI. It was analyzed using a Differential Optical Absorption Spectroscopy (DOAS) method. NO₂ slant column density is the amount of NO₂ found along an average path taken by photons traveling from the sun to the satellite sensor.

  
  
2. Slant column density data was then separated into stratospheric and tropospheric categories based on information coming from the satellite’s data assimilation system. Stratospheric data was then removed from the dataset.

  
  
3. Tropospheric slant column density was converted into tropospheric vertical column density and the average NO₂ density for the entire vertical column was calculated. This was determined by applying an appropriate air mass factor (AMF) and actual, daily information on the vertical distribution of NO₂ calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model. The altitude-dependent AMF used depended on the satellite geometry, terrain height, cloud fraction and height, and surface albedo.

  
  
The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Total Column”.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI).
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. title: Global roads
description:
The Global Roads Inventory Project (GRIP) dataset was developed to provide a more recent and consistent global roads dataset for use in global environmental and biodiversity assessment models. 
 The GRIP dataset is mainly aimed at providing a roads dataset that is easily usable for scientific global environmental and biodiversity modelling projects. The dataset is not suitable for navigation. GRIP4 is based on many different sources (including OpenStreetMap) and to the best of our ability we have verified their public availability, as a criteria in our research. The UNSDI-Transportation datamodel was applied for harmonization of the individual source datasets. 
 We have only included included highways, primary and secondary roads as part of this dataset. The original GRIP dataset consists of tertiary and local roads as well.

description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](2063964b-56c8-4080-b2a5-5a7710f321b9) as a replacement.**_
  
Global Solar Atlas' solar irradiation dataset was developed by Solargis and provided by the World Bank Group. Solar resource, PV power potential, and air temperature data is aggregated long-term into yearly averages. The PV energy simulation is based on the use of re-computed and statistically aggregated 15-minute solar resource and air temperature data. This approach is consistent in terms of space and time, and it is provided as a quick assessment tool for exploration, site prospection and pre-feasibility analysis. The global horizontal irradiation (GHI) reflects the sum of direct and diffuse components of solar radiation.   
  
GHI is one of the principal climate phenomena that determines solar power generation and is considered a climate reference as it enables comparing individual sites or regions. Photovoltaic electricity output, or power potential, is the amount of energy, converted by a PV system into electricity (kWh/kWp) that is expected to be generated according to the geographical conditions of a site and a configuration of the PV system. Three configurations of a PV system are considered: (i) Small residential; (ii) Medium-size commercial; and (iii) Ground-mounted large scale.   
  
The data have a resolution of 1 km and spatial coverage between latitudes 60°N to 45°S. The data represent a time period from January 1994/1999/2007 until December 2015, depending on the satellite coverage. Presently, Solargis processes data from three satellite data providers (EUMETSAT, Japanese Meteorological Agency and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) with geostationary satellites operating at five key positions, to cover the entire world (except polar and subpolar regions). title: Aqueduct Riverine Flood Risk
description:
### Overview  
  
Riverine flood risk measures the percentage of the population expected to be affected by riverine flooding in an average year, accounting for existing flood-protection standards. Higher values indicate that a greater proportion of the population is expected to be impacted by riverine floods on average. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<0.1%) to extremely high (>1%).

  
  
Flood risk was assessed using hazard (inundation caused by river overflow), exposure (population in flood zone), and vulnerability. The existing level of flood protection was also incorporated into the risk calculation. It is important to note that this indicator represents flood risk not in terms of maximum possible impact but rather as average annual impact. The impacts from infrequent, extreme flood years were averaged with more common, less newsworthy flood years to produce the “expected annual affected population.”  Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data on the population impacted by riverine floods were provided by Aqueduct Floods (Ward et al. forthcoming). Flood risk was simulated using a cascade of models within the Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) modeling framework [(Winsemius et al. 2013)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-17-1871-2013). Riverine hazard maps were derived using PCR-GLOBWB 2 inputs from 1960-1999. The riverine flood hazard is represented by inundation maps showing the flood extent and depth for floods of several return periods (2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1000 years) at a horizontal resolution of 5’ x 5’ (regridded to 30” x 30”). Exposure is represented by gridded maps of 2010 population count per cell at a horizontal resolution of 30” x 30". Vulnerability is represented as a binary condition: people are either affected or they are not. Estimates of flood protection standards come from the [FLOPROS model](https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-16-1049-2016). 

  
  
The expected annual affected population was calculated using a risk curve [(Meyer et al. 2009)](https://doi.org/10.1897/IEAM_2008-031.1). To create the curve, the return periods were first converted into probabilities (i.e., 1/return period) and then plotted on the x-axis against the impacted population. Next, flood protection (return year converted to probability) was added to the graph as a vertical line. All impacts that fell to the right of the flood protection line (i.e., impacted by smaller floods) were assumed to be protected against floods and were removed from the calculation. The expected annual affected population was calculated by integrating the area under the curve to the left of the flood protection line.

  
  
The expected annual affected population was divided by total population to calculate the percent of the population expected to be affected annually by riverine floods.

  
  
Finally, raw riverine flood risk values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw riverine flood risk values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.

- Low (0-1): < 0 to 1 in 1,000 people
- Low to medium (1-2): 1 in 1,000 to 2 in 1,000 people
- Medium to high (2-3): 2 in 1,000 to 6 in 1,000 people
- High (3-4): 6 in 1,000 people to 1 in 100 people
- Extremely high (4-5): > 1 in 100 people

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico
description:
### Overview  
  
The Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico dataset provides an estimation of land use land cover (LULC) for nine cities in Mexico. The nine cities are Culiacán, Guadalajara, León, Mérida, Mexico City, Monterrey, Reynosa, Tijuana, and Tuxtla Gutiérrez. Land cover indicates the physical cover over the surface of lands, such as water or vegetation, whereas land use shows how people use the land, such as commercial or plantation. A LULC map classifies areas within a set of categories. This dataset includes the following six categories: Open space, Nonresidential, Residential - Atomistic, Residential - Informal subdivision, Residential - Formal subdivision, and Residential - Housing project. (For full definitions of these categories, see [this working paper](https://marroninstitute.nyu.edu/uploads/content/Measuring_the_Quality_of_Urban_Layouts_December_1_2016_Reduced_new.pdf) or the [technical note](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico).) These "areal" categories exclude the major "linear" urban LULC category: Roads. The data is available for the year 2018 and has a resolution of 5 meters (m).
  
  

The dataset was produced by the World Resources Institute (WRI). It provides an insight into LULC within cities: what lies where and when. This information can play a critical role in urban planning and monitoring. The dataset can be used to measure the impact of different types of urban land use on air quality or identify what types of land use have been affected by natural disasters. Although this particular LULC dataset captures only one moment in time, when available there is also a high value to change detection over time, looking both forward, for planning purposes, and backward, to chart and understand the outcomes of past pressures, development, and policy decisions.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Urban Land Use (Areal) – Mexico dataset was produced in an automated way via supervised machine learning techniques. Automating urban LULC classification reduced the resource and time requirements by orders of magnitude, relative to manual mapping, thus making the process highly scalable. The machine learning model used for classification required two primary ingredients: satellite imagery and ground-truth data. Ground-truth is the observation or measurements about what actually exists at a specific location.This data was collected from the Atlas of Urban Expansion, a multiphase research effort conducted by the New York University (NYU) Urban Expansion Program in partnership with UN-Habitat and the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy. The Sentinel-2 constellation of the European Space Agency was used as the source of satellite imagery. The original resolution of the imagery was 10 m; this was later upsampled to 5 m to utilize as much information as possible from the ground-truth data.
  
  

The satellite imagery was combined with the ground-truth data to create training samples required for training the model. The models were relatively small, straightforward convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The trained models were finally used to map selected cities in Mexico. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [roads](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e1c519d3-16ea-400a-a71c-9033ba5f490b) for the same nine cities in Mexico and LULC (areal) data for [India](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e354f7b8-0fca-422f-bf12-fc6189812bec).

title: Projected Annual Average Temperature U.S. (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps:

All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value.
All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value.
Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2.

The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: [Archived] Malaria Extent
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](3db2f914-2c70-431c-8dce-5dd961bccbd5) as a replacement.**_
  
The Malaria Extent data set is provided by the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) and shows the estimated proportion of 2-10 year olds in the general population that are infected with P. falciparum at any one time on the African continent, where the disease is endemic. Malaria is a disease caused by parasites that are transmitted to humans by Anopheles mosquitoes. Two related parasite species cause the majority of disease and death from malaria: Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. In areas affected by malaria, children and pregnant women are especially vulnerable, a condition further compounded by poverty. In Africa, where 80% of malaria cases are treated at home, the disease kills 1 child in 20 before the age of 5. MAP conducted surveys to collect data on malaria cases. Each survey included in the MAP parasite database has been disaggregated to individual sites (geographical points), individual dates (if the same site was sampled repeatedly), and individual parasite species. Conversely, individual-level survey data have been aggregated up to the community level at a particular site and time. MAP data spans 2000-2015. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Forest Landscape Integrity Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The Forest Landscape Integrity Index (FLII) dataset describes the degree of anthropogenic forest modification as of the beginning of 2019. The dataset is global with 300 m resolution. The FLII was calculated from data covering forest extent, observed and inferred human pressures, and alterations in forest connectivity. 

  
  
Deforestation is a major environmental issue, but far less attention has been given to the degree of anthropogenic modification of remaining forests. Human modification of remaining forests reduces ecosystem integrity, diminishes many of the benefits that these remaining forests provide, and is potentially as significant as outright forest loss in determining overall environmental outcomes. Many global environmental agendas, including halting biodiversity loss, reversing land degradation, and limiting climate change, depend upon retaining forests with high ecological integrity, yet the scale and degree of forest modification remain poorly quantified and mapped. Mapping and monitoring forest modification globally will provide essential information for coordinated global, national, and local policy-making, planning, and action, to help nations and other stakeholders achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and implement other shared commitments.

  
  
Created by [47 forest experts from across the world](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-19493-3#author-information), the FLII offers a timely indicator of the status and management needs of Earth’s remaining forests, and demonstrates there has been a huge loss of forest integrity. Globally, only 17.4 million km2 of forest (40%) can be considered having high integrity and only 27% of this area is found in nationally-designated protected areas ([Grantham et al. 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-19493-3)).
  
  
### Methodology  
  
To produce the Forest Landscape Integrity Index, four datasets were combined representing:
         1. forest extent
        2. ‘observed’ pressure from high impact, localized human activities for which spatial datasets exist, specifically: infrastructure, agriculture, and recent deforestation
3. ‘inferred’ pressure associated with edge effects, and other diffuse processes, (e.g. activities such as hunting and selective logging) modelled using proximity to observed pressures
4. anthropogenic changes in forest connectivity due to forest loss

  
  
These datasets were combined to produce an index score for each forest pixel (300m), with the highest scores reflecting the highest forest integrity, as of the start of 2019.For the full documentation, please see the accompanying article [Grantham et al. 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-19493-3).

title: Water Velocity
description:
Water velocity are two products from the Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM), created by the HYCOM Consortium, the National Ocean Partnership Program (NOPP), and the United States Global Ocean Data Assimilation Experiment (GODEA). HYCOM is a fully three dimensional, multivariate, variational ocean data assimilation system that produces simultaneous analyses of temperature, salinity, geopotential and vector velocity.   
  
The analysis is run in real-time and updates daily. The data have been interpolated to a uniform 0.08 degree lat/long grid between 80.48°S and 80.48°N. The salinity, temperature, and velocity variables have been interpolated to 40 standard z-levels (vertical depth).   
  
The high resolution makes HYCOM eddy resolving. Eddy-resolving models can more accurately simulate western boundary currents and the associated mesoscale variability and they better maintain more accurate and sharper ocean fronts. In particular, an eddy resolving ocean model allows upper ocean topographic coupling via flow instabilities. The coupling occurs when flow instabilities drive abyssal currents that in turn steer the pathways of upper ocean currents. In ocean prediction this coupling is important for ocean model dynamical interpolation skill in data assimilation/nowcasting and in ocean forecasting, which is feasible on time scales up to about a month.

Projected Extreme Heat Days (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset shows the change in the average number of days of extreme heat at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme heat day is a day where the maximum temperature is greater than the 99th percentile maximum temperature during the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. Temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, an increased quantity of extreme heat days can lead to human and ecosystem threats caused by more frequent, more intense, and longer heat waves.

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The average number of extreme heat days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily maximum temperature values for a given year and summing the number of days where the maximum temperature was greater than the 99th percentile temperature during the baseline period. The number of extreme heat days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in extreme heat days. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Global Terrorism Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Terrorism Index (GTI) is a quantification of the impact of terrorism in a country. It provides a comprehensive summary of the key global trends and patterns in terrorism over the last 50 years. A higher GTI represents a higher impact of terrorism in a country.

  
  
 GTI measures the impact of terrorism in a country by combining data for all terrorist incidents occuring in a country for a given year. Each possible terrorist event is analyzed to make sure it is within GTI’s requirements to be qualified as a terrorist incident and is given a score based on four indicators.

  
  
The Global Terrorism Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace (IEP) using data from the Global Terrorism Database (GTD) and other sources. Data for the GTD was collected and composed by the National Consortium for the Study of Terrorism and Responses to Terrorism (START) at the University of Maryland. 

  
  
The GTI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2002 to 2018 for 163 countries or independent territories covering 99.7% of the world’s population. This data can help to create a discussion about the future of terrorism and the necessary policy measures to mitigate it.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Global Terrorism Index (GTI) utilzed data from the Global Terorism Database, which has information on 170,000 terrorist incidents from 1970 to the end of 2018. The GTI dataset contains information  from 2012 to 2018. Three criteria were used to determine whether an incident qualified to be included in the Global Terrorism Database. To be included in the database the incident had to meet the points outlined below:

  
  
1. The incident was intentional - the result of a conscious calculation on the part of a perpetrator.
  
  
2. The incident involved some level of violence or threat of violence - including property damage as well as violence against people.
  
  
3. The perpetrators of the incidents were sub-national actors. This database did not include acts of state terrorism.

  
  
 Incidents with insufficient information were not included in the database. 

  
  
The GTI was developed in consultation with the Global Peace Index Expert Panel. Country scores were calculated on a scale from 0 to 10; where 0 represented no impact from terrorism and 10 represented the highest measurable impact of terrorism. Scores were determined by analyzing each terrorism incident using four indicators:

- total number of terrorist incidents in a given year 
- total number of fatalities caused by terrorists in a given year 
- total number of injuries caused by terrorists in a given year
- a measure of the total property damage from terrorist incidents in a given year


  
  
Each indicator was given a different weight between zero and three for every incident, and a five year weighted average was applied to the country score to reflect the long term psychological impact of terrorist incidents. Psychological impacts of terrorist incidents often last in a society for many years after the incident.  Finally, a base 10 logarithmic banding system between 0 and 10, at 0.5 intervals, was applied to each country score to get the final GTI value. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/11/GTI-2019web.pdf)

title: Average Low Temperature
description:
Annual average low temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

Commercial Shipping Lanes
description:
### Overview  
  
The Commercial Shipping Lanes dataset shows heavily trafficked shipping routes around the world. The shipping lanes were generated from GPS location data collected by 3,374 commercial and research vessels from October 2004 - October 2005. The data points from all ships were combined to form tracks of shipping lanes around the world with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km). Shipping lanes are colored by density of ship traffic, with bright-colored lanes representing high volumes of ship traffic and dark-colored lanes representing low volumes of ship traffic. 

  
  
The Commercial Shipping Lanes dataset can be used to identify areas that are exposed to high levels of shipping traffic and potential environmental impacts. Shipping traffic can be disruptive to the environment in many ways, including noise pollution, fuel pollution and ballast water discharge. Many marine animals rely on sound for communication, navigation and locating prey. Noise pollution from shipping activities can [interfere with their ability to hear](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ocean-noise.html), negatively impacting animals and ocean ecosystems. [Pollution from fuel spills](https://www.noaa.gov/education/resource-collections/ocean-coasts/oil-spills) and emissions harms the health of the ocean. Ballast water, water that is taken on in port to help stabilize a ship, is often discharged once a ship has unloaded its cargo. Ballast water can contain plants and animals, [including invasive species](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/subject/ballast-water&sa=D&ust=1606947117838000&usg=AOvVaw2x2V2C6SjLO0CwU6UO4A8C), that can be harmful when introduced to a new ocean ecosystem. 

  
  
The Commercial Shipping Lanes data set was created by the [National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS)](https://www.nceas.ucsb.edu/about), an independent research affiliate of the University of California, Santa Barbara. This dataset was part of NCEAS’s [Global Map of Human Impacts on Marine Ecosystems](https://www.nceas.ucsb.edu/globalmarine), an assessment of cumulative human impacts on the ocean. The Commercial Shipping Lanes dataset is distributed by the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/) as part of its [Science on a Sphere initiative](https://sos.noaa.gov/What_is_SOS/). GPS data was retrieved from the [International Comprehensive Ocean-Atmosphere Data Set (ICOADS)](https://icoads.noaa.gov/), a digital dataset of weather observations collected on ships. The GPS data used for the Commercial Shipping Lanes dataset was provided by the [World Meteorological Organization’s Voluntary Observing Ship (VOS Scheme)](http://sot.jcommops.org/vos/vos.html). Ships participating in the VOS Scheme opt to carry monitoring equipment and periodically report measurements on their location and environmental variables such as sea surface temperature, wind direction, and speed.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Ship location data was collected by 3,374 commercial and research ships from October 2004 - October 2005. Data was collected by the VOS Scheme, a voluntary weather observation program, and represented approximately 11% of the ships at sea in 2005. Ships reported their locations four times each day, at 0000, 0600, 1200 and 1800 UTC. A total of 1,189,127 data points were collected. Ship tracks were colored according to density, where brighter colors represent higher density of ship traffic. The density of ship tracks ranged from 1-1,158 ships.

title: [Archived] FORMA Active Clearing Alerts
description:
Unlike other forest change data on Global Forest Watch, which only allow a single alert per pixel, FORMA active clearing alerts show areas of likely change from the last month, week, or 48 hours without considering previous alerts. This means that an alert detected this month that has had previous loss will be picked up by the FORMA active clearing alerts, but not by other products. FORMA alerts are processed in Google Earth Engine (GEE) using a combination of two MODIS products: NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index), and FIRMS (Fires Information for Resource Management System). NDVI updates are processed every 16 days, while fire updates are processed daily. Models are developed individually for each ecogroup to relate the two inputs to the area of clearing, using the Hansen annual tree cover loss data to train the model. The minimum threshold to qualify as an alert is 25% of the pixel cleared, though thresholds vary by ecogroup to minimize false positives.

title: Costa Rica Projected Coffee Suitability
description:
The Coffee Suitability Projections Under Four Scenarios data set was produced by Centro Internacional de Agricultura Tropical (CIAT) and shows coffee suitability projections. It was created as part of a study that attempts to utilize data from four Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) emissions scenarios (RCP 2.6, 4.5, 6.0, and 8.5) in two time periods (2050 and 2080) to determine the impact of climate change on coffee cultivation in coffee growing regions of Costa Rica. The study was done using georeferenced points obtained from Instituto del Café de Costa Rica (ICAFE), and using the MaxEnt model to simulate the adaptability of coffee production. 

Environmental layers taken into account comprise 19 bioclimatic variables from the Worldclim database. Developed by Hijmans et al. 2005, thousands of data points from meteorological stations around the world were collected for the time period of 1960 to 1990, using an interpolation to create environmental layers (rasters) of average temperature with 24,542 locations, minimum and maximum temperatures with 14,835 locations, and precipitation with 47,554 locations. These were all calculated by month, with a resolution of 1 square km. Bioclimatic variables were derived from monthly temperature and precipitation values with the goal of generating biologically significant and indispensable variables so that cultivation may develop properly.

PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

Urban Land Use (Roads) - Mexico
description:
### Overview  
  
The Urban Land Use (Roads) – Mexico dataset provides an estimation of land use land cover (LULC) for nine cities in Mexico. The nine cities are Culiacán, Guadalajara, León, Mérida, Mexico City, Monterrey, Reynosa, Tijuana, and Tuxtla Gutiérrez. Land cover indicates the physical cover over the surface of lands, such as water or vegetation, whereas land use shows how people use the land, such as commercial or plantation. A LULC map classifies areas within a set of categories. This dataset includes only roads, which were classified separately from other types of LULC in order to achieve the best possible results. The data is available for the year 2018 and has a resolution of 5 meters (m).
  
  

The dataset was produced by the World Resources Institute (WRI). It provides an insight into LULC within cities: what lies where and when. This information can play a critical role in urban planning and monitoring. This dataset can be used to measure the impact of different types of urban land use on air quality or identify what types of land use have been affected by natural disasters. Although this particular LULC dataset is just one point in time, when available there is also a high value to change detection over time, looking both forward, for planning purposes, and backward, to chart and understand the outcomes of past pressures, development, and policy decisions.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Urban Land Use (Roads) – Mexico dataset was produced in an automated way via supervised machine learning techniques. Automating urban LULC classification helped in reducing the resource and time requirements by orders of magnitude, thus making the process highly scalable. The machine learning model used for classification required two primary ingredients: satellite imagery and ground-truth data. Ground-truth is the observation or measurements about what actually exists at a specific location. This data was collected from the Atlas of Urban Expansion, a multiphase research effort conducted by the New York University (NYU) Urban Expansion Program in partnership with UN-Habitat and the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy. Sentinel-2 imagery from the European Space Agency was used as the source of satellite imagery. The original resolution of the imagery was 10 m, which was later upsampled to 5 m to utilize maximum information from the ground truth data.
  
  

The satellite imagery was combined with the ground-truth data to create training samples required for training the model. The models were relatively small, straightforward convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The trained models were finally used to map selected cities in Mexico. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/mapping-urban-land-use-in-india-and-mexico).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [areal LULC](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/dfbf97c3-ee82-4c68-808b-3bcc60e57167) for the same nine cities in Mexico and for [urban India](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e354f7b8-0fca-422f-bf12-fc6189812bec).

Urban Extent for Select Cities
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the physical urban extent and population of a global random sample of 200 cities, circa 2014. The urban extent of a city was defined as the extent of a city’s contiguous built-up area. While these extents can cover large areas and multiple municipalities, they often represent one shared labor market. 

  
  
This dataset was created as part of the Atlas of Urban Expansion, which aims to monitor both the quantitative and qualitative aspects of urban expansion using a globally representative sample of 200 cities. Having the physical extents of a large sample of global cities provides a powerful tool to analyze urbanization trends on a global scale. In addition to monitoring the urban extent of these cities, this dataset includes information on the population, built-up area, walkability, and numerous other variables. The data source also provides data for urban extents circa 1990 and circa 2000.

  
  
This dataset was published by the New York University Urban Expansion Program at the Marron Institute of Urban Management and the Stern School of Business of New York University, in partnership with UN-Habitat and the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy.   
  
### Methodology  
  
To create this dataset, the authors first identified cities that had a population of 100,000 or more people. They compiled 2010 population data for cities across the world, using population data from the United Nations Population Division and the [City Population website](http://www.citypopulation.de/). They identified 4,231 global cities that met this criterion.

  
  
The authors then selected the 200 cities included in this dataset with a stratified sampling method, which  was used to ensure that cities of varying sizes, from all regions, and from large and small countries were well-represented. Cities were randomly selected from eight world regions in proportion to the urban population in each region. The eight world regions were
- East Asia and Pacific; 
- Southeast Asia; 
- South and Central Asia; 
- Western Asia and North Africa; 
- Sub-Saharan Africa; 
- Latin America and the Caribbean;
- Europe and Japan; and 
- Land-Rich Developed countries 

  
  
After selecting a representative sample of 200 cities, researchers identified the urban extent of each city. The urban extent was defined as the extent of a city’s built-up area, rather than by its administrative or jurisdictional boundaries.  Each urban extent can cover a large area of land and multiple municipalities, but often share  a single labor market. The geographical extent is typically associated with the name of its largest and most prominent historical center. Researchers created the urban extent data by digitizing and analyzing high-resolution satellite imagery. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.lincolninst.edu/sites/default/files/pubfiles/atlas-of-urban-expansion-2016-volume-1-full.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the average population density of city extent, the fragmentation of the built-up area by open spaces, the compactness of the overall geographic shape, and the shares of infill, extension, leapfrog, and inclusion in the added built-up areas within new urban extent is available from the data provider. This data is available for three time periods: circa 1990, circa 2000, and circa 2014. Data related to blocks and roads is also available. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This dataset was retrieved from AidData GeoQuery. The general steps used to download this dataset are described [here](https://www.aiddata.org/blog/urban-boundaries-for-200-cities-added-to-aiddatas-geoquery-tool), and the specific query used to download the data shown on Resource Watch can be found [here](http://geo.aiddata.org/query/#!/search/atlasofurbanexpansion2016/atlasofurbanexpansion2016_urban_edge_t3).

description:

This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis and Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, the U.S. Geological Survey, and  the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, measures areas of tree cover gain across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at 30 × 30 m resolution, displayed as a 12-year cumulative layer. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+) sensor. Over 600,000 Landsat 7 images were compiled and analyzed using Google Earth Engine, a cloud platform for Earth observation and data analysis. The clear land surface observations (30 × 30 m pixels) in the satellite images were assembled, and a supervised learning algorithm was then applied to identify per pixel tree cover gain. Tree cover gain was defined as the establishment of tree canopy at the Landsat pixel scale in an area that previously had no tree cover. Tree cover gain may indicate a number of potential activities, including natural forest growth or the crop rotation cycle of tree plantations. The tree cover canopy density of the displayed data is >50%. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Riverine Nitrogen (N) and Phosphorus (P) Input, Retention, and Export
description:
The Integrated Model to Assess the Global Environment—Global Nutrient Model (IMAGE-GNM) is a global distributed, spatially explicit model using hydrology as the basis for describing nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) delivery to surface water, transport, and in-stream retention in rivers, lakes, wetlands, and reservoirs. It is part of the integrated assessment model IMAGE, which studies the interaction between society and the environment over prolonged time periods. In the IMAGE-GNM model, grid cells receive water with dissolved and suspended N and P from upstream grid cells; inside grid cells, N and P are delivered to water bodies via diffuse sources (surface runoff, shallow and deep groundwater, riparian zones, litterfall in floodplains, atmospheric deposition) and point sources (wastewater); N and P retention in a water body is calculated on the basis of the residence time of the water and nutrient uptake velocity; subsequently, water and nutrients are transported to downstream grid cells. Differences between model results and observed concentrations for a range of global rivers are acceptable given the global scale of the uncalibrated model. Sensitivity analysis with data for the year 2000 showed that runoff is a major factor for N and P delivery, retention, and river export. For both N and P, uptake velocity and all factors used to compute the subgrid in-stream retention are important for total in-stream retention and river export. Soil N budgets, wastewater, and all factors determining litterfall in floodplains are important for N delivery to surface water. For P the factors that determine the P content of the soil (soil P content and bulk density) are important factors for delivery and river export. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The GLIMS: Global Glacier Database managed by the NSIDC is an international collaborative project that includes more than 60 institutions worldwide. Its goal is to create this globally comprehensive inventory of land ice including measurements of glacier area, geometry, surface velocity, and snow line elevation. To perform these analyses, the GLIMS project uses satellite data, primarily from the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) and the Landsat Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+), as well as historical information derived from maps and aerial photographs. The analysis results are submitted to the GLIMS database at the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) in Boulder, CO. The GLIMS database is designed to be a logical extension of the World Glacier Inventory (WGI) of the World Glacier Monitoring Service (WGMS) and stores the full complement of the WGMS-defined glacier characteristics. Each analysis received by the GLIMS team at the NSIDC is ingested into the GLIMS Glacier Database. New glacier data are continually being added to the database. title: [Archived] Coral Reef Bleaching Alerts
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](574f0b71-8363-4e3a-978f-2b1ce58c1c33) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
The Coral Reef Bleaching Alerts dataset shows the maximum amount of coral bleaching stress that an area has experienced over the past seven day period. The dataset is based on bleaching stress caused by high sea surface temperatures (SST). Bleaching stress is determined by comparing historical SST data to near-real-time SST data to view ocean areas that have potentially harmful heat stress levels, especially with regard to accumulated heat stress impacts. For this dataset SST information is used to classify ocean areas into five bleaching alert categories: no stress, bleaching watch, bleaching warning (bleaching is possible), bleaching alert level 1 (bleaching is likely to occur), and bleaching alert level 2 (coral death is likely to occur). The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 5 kilometers (km) and is available for all of earth’s oceans. It is updated daily and displays the highest bleaching alert category the ocean pixel has experience within the last seven days.

  
  
Coral reefs provide economic goods and services worth about $375 billion each year and are home to over 25% of all marine life. Coral bleaching occurs when a coral expels its symbiotic dinoflagellates  (zooxanthellae) due to various environmental stresses. After zooxanthellae are expelled only a white skeleton remains; this phenomenon is known as bleaching. Increased SST of as little as 1 to 2 degrees celsius above normal has been shown to cause bleaching. Extensive bleaching events have dramatic long-term ecological and social impacts, including loss of reef-building corals, changes in benthic habitat, changes in associated fish populations, and economic loss. After a bleaching event it can take decades for severely bleached reefs to fully recover. As the climate continues to warm, bleaching is a major threat to the future of coral reefs.

  
  
The dataset was created by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data and Information Service (NESDIS) as part of their Coral Reef Watch program. The dataset has proven highly successful in nowcasting mass coral bleaching episodes. It provides reliable global monitoring and prediction of environmental conditions leading to bleaching and is used to guide targeted observations and management responses around the world.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Coral Reef Bleaching Alerts dataset shown on Resource Watch utilizes the NOAA Coral Reef Watch (CRW) daily global 5 km satellite Bleaching Alert Area (7-day maximum) product. It was created by comparing near-real-time sea surface temperature (SST) values with a long-term baseline SST (climatology). The climatology was produced using night-only values for the period 1985–2012 from the 4-km AVHRR Pathfinder Version 5.2 SST (PFV5.2), an official NOAA climate data record.  For each pixel (4 km), daily SST data were averaged for each month to produce monthly composites. These were then averaged across the 28-year period to produce 12 monthly mean climatologies. 
  
  
Near-real-time SST values were taken from NOAA National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service (NESDIS) near-real-time operational daily global 5-km Geo-Polar Blended Night-Only SST Analysis. This NESDIS data is derived from SST measurements taken by a combination of six satellites (four geostationary and two polar-orbiting satellites) operated by NOAA, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) and the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMETSAT). The satellites take as many as 50 SST observations each night over the same location. The final daily SST value for each pixel is a combination of all SST measurements taken each night.

  
  
Daily SST values were compared to monthly mean climatology to determine anomalies (differences) in daily SSTs. From this information two measurements were created: Coral Bleaching HotSpots and Degree Heating Weeks (DHW). Coral Bleaching HotSpots is a measurement of the magnitude of daily thermal stress that can lead to coral bleaching. It describes the amount of degrees that a daily SST value is higher than the maximum of the monthly mean (MMM) climatology for a pixel. The MMM climatology for any given pixel is the maximum value among the 12-monthly mean SST climatologies for that grid cell. DHW shows the accumulated thermal stress over a prolonged period and has been shown to be predictive of mass coral bleaching. It is an accumulation of all daily HotSpot values that are at least 1°C, over a 12-week period. The final Bleaching Alert Area (BAA) (7-day maximum) dataset is derived from a combination of DHW and HotSpot data. BAA is updated daily, but shows the maximum Alert Level of the preceding seven days. BAA levels are assigned using the following criteria:

- No Stress: HotSpot <=0
- Bleaching Watch: 0<HotSpot<1
- Bleaching Warning (possible bleaching): 1<= HotSpot and 0<DHW<4
- Bleaching Alert Level 1 (bleaching likely): 1<=HotSpot and 4<=DHW<8
- Bleaching Alert Level 2 (mortality likely): 1<=HotSpot and 8<=DHW

For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

Additional data for sea surface temperature, sea surface temperature anomaly, coral bleaching hotspots, degree heating week, bleaching alert area (single-day), and sea surface temperature trend (7-day) are available from the data provider. title: Cruise Ports
description:
### Overview  
  
The Cruise Ports dataset shows the number of visitors received by ports worldwide from July 2009 - June 2010. This dataset is part of the [Reefs at Risk Revisited](https://www.wri.org/publication/reefs-risk-revisited) report from World Resources Institute (WRI). Cruise port and passenger volume data was provided to WRI by [Clean Cruising](https://www.cleancruising.com.au/), a commercial cruise booking company based in Brisbane, Australia. 

  
  
Cruise ships can be a significant source of air and water pollution. According to a 2010 report from [Cruise Lines International Association](https://cruising.org/en/), a typical one-week cruise on a large ship (3,000 passengers and crew) generates almost 800 cubic meters of sewage; 3,700 cubic meters of graywater; half a cubic meter of hazardous waste; 8 tons of solid waste; and nearly 100 cubic meters of oily bilge water. Pollution from cruise ships can threaten coral reef health, particularly in the Atlantic where there are a large number of cruise ship ports. Cruise ships also produce harmful greenhouse gas emissions and can disturb marine wildlife. These problems are exacerbated in ports where several ships are frequently docked. Identifying locations and volume of cruise ship passengers can provide insight on where to expect environmental impacts to water and air quality at ports. The Cruise Ports dataset can also help inform environmental policy decisions in areas that receive high volumes of cruise ship passengers.  

  
  
The Cruise Ports dataset was provided by [WRI](https://www.wri.org/about), an independent, non-governmental global research organization that seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. WRI was founded in 1982 to address the environmental issues of deforestation, desertification and climate change. They use a science and evidence-based approach to achieve global change. WRI conducts independent research, tests ideas with leaders of cities, companies and countries, and implements proven ideas to transform societies and economies.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Cruise Ports dataset was generated by cruise port and passenger volume data provided by Clean Cruising. Passenger volume data was compiled from booking and departure information for all major cruise lines between July 2009 - June 2010. Port locations were mapped using the [National Geospatial Intelligence Agency World Port Index](https://msi.nga.mil/Publications/WPI.0).

  
  
The Cruise Ports dataset was part of the Reefs at Risk Revisited report from WRI. For the full documentation, please see the source [technical documentation](https://www.wri.org/publication/reefs-risk-revisited).

title: Average High Temperature
description:
Annual average high temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Access to an Improved Water Source (National)
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset includes the percentage of people using drinking water from an improved source that is accessible, available when needed, and free from contamination. It provides values for the years 2000 to 2017, at the country level. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), safely managed drinking water is defined as an improved water source that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from fecal and priority chemical contamination. Improved water sources include piped water, boreholes or tubewells, protected dug wells, protected springs, and packaged and delivered water.

  
  
WHO and UNICEF’s Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene prepared this dataset. Access to safe drinking water is a human right, not a privilege, for everyone. Access to safe water can reduce illness and death from disease, improve health, reduce poverty, and lead to socioeconomic development. Yet many countries still lack access to safe drinking water. Children are especially vulnerable to deaths and illnesses related to lack of access to proper drinking water services. In addition, women and girls are almost two and a half times more likely than men and boys to fetch water, reducing their time for other activities, such as attending school. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was developed based on administrative sources, national censuses, and nationally representative surveys. A weighted average was calculated to aggregate subnational data to the national level. There are three criteria for an improved water source: (1) accessibility: water should be accessible on the premises, (2) availability: water should be available when needed, and (3) quality: water supplied should be free from contamination. The WHO/UNICEF JMP provides national estimates only when data is available on drinking water quality and at least one of the criteria (accessibility and availability).

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://databank.worldbank.org/reports.aspx?source=2&type=metadata&series=SH.H2O.SMDW.ZS).

title: Urban Land Use (Areal) – India
description:
### Overview  
  
The Urban Land Use (Areal) – India dataset provides an estimation of land use land cover (LULC) for urban spaces in India. Maps are available for the years 2016 and 2019. Land cover indicates the physical cover over the surface of lands, such as water or vegetation, whereas land use shows how people use the land, such as commercial or plantation. A LULC map classifies areas within a set of categories. This dataset includes the following six categories: Open space, Nonresidential, Residential - Atomistic, Residential - Informal subdivision, Residential - Formal subdivision, and Residential - Housing project. These "areal" categories exclude the major "linear" urban LULC category: Roads. The final product has a resolution of 5 meters (m).
  
  

The dataset was produced by the World Resources Institute (WRI). It provides an insight into LULC within cities: what lies where and when. This information can play a critical role in urban planning and monitoring. Example uses might be measuring the impact of different types of urban land use on air quality or identifying what types of land use have been affected by disasters. There is also a high value to change detection over time, looking both forward, for planning purposes, and backward, to chart and understand the outcomes of past pressures, development, and policy decisions.

title: Air Quality: Mexico City Carbon Monoxide (CO) Forecast
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Mexico City Carbon Monoxide (CO) Forecast dataset provides weather and air quality forecasts for Mexico City. This dataset represents the forecasted density of Carbon Monoxide in parts per billion (ppb). The forecast offers an hourly estimate on Carbon Monoxide density with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km), encompassing Mexico CIty and its Metropolitan Area (MCMA).

  
  
According to the [U.S. Center for Disease Control (CDC)](https://www.cdc.gov/co/faqs.htm), CO is released when fossil fuels are burned. Common household sources include grills, cars, fireplaces, and gas stoves that aren’t properly ventilated. Major sources of CO to outdoor air include cars, trucks and other fossil-fuel-burning machinery. Breathing air with a high concentration of carbon monoxide reduces oxygen availability in the bloodstream for critical organs like the heart and brain. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion. As stated by [Mexico City Ministry of the Environment (SEDEMA)](http://www.aire.cdmx.gob.mx/descargas/publicaciones/flippingbook/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017/mobile/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017v3.pdf), the CO values in Mexico City have been decreasing over the last years, complying with the levels set by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the World Health Organization (WHO). The main source of CO in the MCMA is fossil-fuel-burning related to transport, making this pollutant a good indicator to monitor transport-related emissions in the region. Showcasing the spatial distribution of CO in the MCMA will  provide insight about the way a city can produce information according to its needs while complementing global air quality models.The forecast helps the Mexico CIty government to issue health warnings based on the expected air quality for a given day, like recommending citizens to avoid open-air exercise or to limit their use of fossil fuel vehicles.

  
  
The forecast was generated by SEDEMA with help from the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). SEDEMA provides a tool for the inhabitants of MCMA to make well-informed decisions about dangerous air pollution activity on a given day. SEDEMA works on five environmental issues: air quality and climate change, land conservation and biodiversity, sustainable urban infrastructure, water supply and quality, and environmental communication and education.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The dataset is comprised of the following models:
  
  
Weather: Estimates the weather conditions of the MCMA using data from global systems. It harnesses the [Weather Research and Forecasting Model-Advanced Research (WRF-ARW)](https://www.mmm.ucar.edu/weather-research-and-forecasting-model), which is a mesoscale numerical weather prediction system designed for both atmospheric research and operational forecasting applications. The model generates  temperature, wind, rainfall and solar radiation, among other weather related indicators..
  
  
Emissions: This model makes use of emission inventories for the MCMA to estimate CO levels on an hourly basis, as well as its geospatial distribution.
  
  
Chemical Transport: This model harnesses the outputs from the weather and emissions models as well as other chemical and physical mechanisms to simulate transformations in the atmosphere and the influence of weather dynamics in these processes. For this purpose, the [Community Multiscale Air Quality Modeling System (CMAQ)](https://www.cmascenter.org/cmaq/) is employed to forecast the behavior of the pollutants in the MCMA.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows forecasts for [Air Quality: Mexico City Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) forecast ](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/59790e64-d95d-43fa-a124-5c7eb1cb4456), [Air Quality: Mexico City Ozone  (O₃)Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/00d6bae1-e105-4165-8230-ee73a8128538), [Air Quality: Mexico City Nitrogen Dioxide  (NO₂) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/918ba6bc-69ed-44fb-9b29-5fb445fdfef6), and [Air Quality: Mexico City Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7a34b770-83f9-4c6a-acb8-31edcff7241e)
